idiom_name: handle/body with a sharing count and detach on first write
implementation_notes: Language-neutral blueprint: split the value into a small handle and a heap body; the handle holds the sharing state (a count, an explicit shared flag, or a uniqueness test) plus a pointer to the body. Every mutating operation first checks whether the body is shared and, if it is, clones the body, rebinds the handle and releases the old reference; reads never touch the count. Release must be deterministic if the count is what triggers the free - otherwise the count degenerates into a flag and a garbage collector reclaims the body. Detaching is the whole contract: if any mutation path can reach the body without going through the detach step, the type silently stops being a value.
code_sketch:
class Cow:                          # cheap handle; copy() shares the body
    def __init__(self, body, shared=False):
        self._body, self._shared = body, shared
    def __copy__(self):             # both handles now share the body
        other = Cow(self._body, shared=True)
        self._shared = True
        return other
    def _detach(self):              # first writer clones
        if self._shared:
            self._body, self._shared = clone(self._body), False
    def mutate(self, op):
        self._detach(); op(self._body)
pitfalls: Detaching on reads 'to be safe' throws the optimization away; detach only in the logically mutating operations.
A shallow copy of the body leaves nested state shared, reintroducing the aliasing bug one level down.
Copying the handle without marking both handles shared lets the first writer mutate in place.
With a garbage-collected runtime the count cannot trigger the free: replace it with an explicit shared/frozen flag or the bookkeeping is wasted.

The use_count() == 1 check for uniqueness is racy between threads: between the check and the write, another thread may acquire a reference; use compare_exchange or a lock around the entire detach+write sequence in multithreaded code.
Interior references (iterators, pointers into the body) dangle after detach: prevent their escape from the type's interface, or mark unshareable the moment a reference escapes.
GC collectors that mark by traversing every object (mark-and-sweep) dirty every COW-shared page, causing forked processes to copy their entire heap on the next GC cycle even when doing no work.

Wrong move: giving a copy-on-write type reference- or pointer-yielding accessors the way pre-C++11 std::string handed out char& and data() -> callers mutate the shared body without ever running the detach (and C++11's O(1) non-const-access rule makes a correct detach there impossible, which is why COW std::string was banned) -> instead only COW types that never hand out interior mutable references, and expose non-owning views (string_view-style) for read access.

Wrong move: making strings/containers copy-on-write inside a multithreaded process because 'the refcount check is cheap' -> every copy and destroy becomes an atomic read-modify-write and some commercial implementations took a hidden lock per operation, so the cache line holding the count ping-pongs across cores and the 'optimization' costs more than the copy it avoided (Sutter, Optimizations That Aren't) -> instead share immutable snapshots behind shared_ptr/Arc and swap in a whole new value on write.

Wrong move: reasoning about copies of a COW value by pointer equality or by watching addresses in the debugger -> two handles may share one body or diverge at an invisible detach, so 'same address' stops meaning 'same value' and aliasing bugs look like memory corruption -> instead compare by value equality only, and temporarily swap in a non-COW build of the type when hunting an aliasing bug.
